reasoning_traces.think:
The core idea of inference-time Nash alignment is to compute a Nash equilibrium in a two-player zero-sum game between policies, where one player seeks to maximize expected preference satisfaction while the other minimizes it. This formulation allows for alignment under general preferences that do not reduce to scalar Bradley-Terry rewards. The Best-of-Nash (BoN) method draws N responses from a reference policy π_ref, constructs an empirical preference matrix, and solves a linear program to find the optimal policy distribution. The Nash Mirror Descent (NMD) approach uses self-play dynamics to iteratively refine policy estimates. Both methods rely on the duality gap to quantify how close the current policy is to equilibrium. Theorems establish bounds on this gap, showing that increasing N reduces the gap to within ε(x)C_uni(x), indicating convergence. These primitives enable robust policy alignment without retraining, leveraging game-theoretic principles to optimize complex, multi-dimensional preferences.
